# Caminito

Take a stroll through Buenos Aires' famously colourful street museum.

![...](https://turismo.buenosaires.gob.ar/sites/turismo/files/calle-museo-caminito-dic2025-1500x610.jpg)

![...](https://turismo.buenosaires.gob.ar/sites/turismo/files/2caminito-aerea-1500x610.jpg)

### Present in tours

[La Boca](/en/recorrido/la-boca) |

[Markets and fairs](/en/recorrido/markets-and-fairs) |

[Must-see attractions](/en/recorrido/must-see-attractions) |

Located in La boca, the Caminito (little path, in Spanish) is a street museum of colourful painted houses typical of the immigrant dwellings that came to chracterise this portside area towards the end of the 19th and start of the 20th century.

The Caminito followed the route of an old stream that once flowed into the Riachuelo, and later, after the river dried up, formed part of a railroad route. After the closure of the railroad, the street was largely abandoned until in the 1950s a group of neighbours decided to regenerate the area and local artist Benito Quinquela Martín began using the tenements as his canvas.

Today, there are several works by Argentine artists incorporated as part of the street museum and the Caminito has become a favourite with visitors to the city. Several restaurants offer tango and folk dance shows and street fills with artists offering original crafts and paintings.

The tenement buildings made of wood and sheet metal are typical of the *conventillos*, precarious, communal dwellings built by Genoan immigrants starting in the late 19th century. Many dwellings are built on raised foundations due to frequent floods in the past.

# SAN TELMO + CAMINITO THE LOCAL WALKING TOUR!

REVIEW · BUENOS AIRES

# SAN TELMO + CAMINITO THE LOCAL WALKING TOUR!

Operated by Cachalote tours · Bookable on GetYourGuide

This walk connects old Buenos Aires to tango. You’ll move between **San Telmo** and **Caminito** in a way that feels like you’re reading the city with your feet, not just snapping pictures, with colonial streets, immigrant-era stories, and local rhythm along the way.

I love how the guide ties what you see to why it matters: Spanish-colonial style buildings that date back around **400 years**, plus narrow streets where tango and artisan life show up in everyday details. I also love that the included **mate** ritual isn’t treated like a checkbox, it’s explained so you know what you’re looking at.

One thing to plan for: it’s mostly on foot, so bring **comfortable shoes** and expect a solid walking day. It’s also not listed as suitable for babies under 1 year or people over 70.

In This Review

## Key highlights to look for

![SAN TELMO + CAMINITO THE LOCAL WALKING TOUR! - Key highlights to look for](https://9.buenosairestravelguide.com/wp-content/uploads/san-telmo-caminito-the-local-walking-tour-1.jpg)

![SAN TELMO + CAMINITO THE LOCAL WALKING TOUR! - Key highlights to look for](https://9.buenosairestravelguide.com/wp-content/uploads/san-telmo-caminito-the-local-walking-tour-1.jpg)

## San Telmo + Caminito in one afternoon: the smart way to get oriented

![SAN TELMO + CAMINITO THE LOCAL WALKING TOUR! - San Telmo + Caminito in one afternoon: the smart way to get oriented](https://9.buenosairestravelguide.com/wp-content/uploads/san-telmo-caminito-the-local-walking-tour-2.jpg)  
This is the kind of tour that helps you understand Buenos Aires fast. Instead of bouncing between random stops, you’ll get a clear contrast: **San Telmo** as the older spine of the city, and **Caminito** as the colorful, immigrant-driven neighborhood story where tango took shape at the end of the 1800s.

![SAN TELMO + CAMINITO THE LOCAL WALKING TOUR! - San Telmo + Caminito in one afternoon: the smart way to get oriented](https://9.buenosairestravelguide.com/wp-content/uploads/san-telmo-caminito-the-local-walking-tour-2.jpg)

The tour runs as a small-group experience, limited to **10 participants**, and that matters. In a group that size, your guide can actually point out details in the street level stuff, like architectural clues, not just talk at you from a distance. Plus, you’re walking through both areas in about **3 hours**, with a bus segment that keeps you from spending the day figuring out transit.

At **$35 per person** with a guide in English or Spanish, plus **bus tickets** and the **mate** ritual demonstration, the value is mostly in the storytelling and navigation. This isn’t a museum day, and it’s not designed to hand you lunch on a tray. It’s built for learning the city through neighborhood rhythm.

![](https://9.buenosairestravelguide.com/wp-content/uploads/nazis-in-buenos-aires-a-historical-walking-tour-150x150.jpg)
![](https://9.buenosairestravelguide.com/wp-content/uploads/buenos-aires-personalized-2-to-8-hour-private-walking-tour-150x150.jpg)

## Starting at the Mafalda bench: a meeting point that actually helps

![SAN TELMO + CAMINITO THE LOCAL WALKING TOUR! - Starting at the Mafalda bench: a meeting point that actually helps](https://9.buenosairestravelguide.com/wp-content/uploads/san-telmo-caminito-the-local-walking-tour.jpg)  
You’ll meet at the **touristic bench from the Mafalda cartoon**, right at the **Estatua de Mafalda**. I like meeting points like this because you don’t waste time hunting down a “nearby landmark” that could be anywhere. You can show up, regroup, and get started.

![SAN TELMO + CAMINITO THE LOCAL WALKING TOUR! - Starting at the Mafalda bench: a meeting point that actually helps](https://9.buenosairestravelguide.com/wp-content/uploads/san-telmo-caminito-the-local-walking-tour.jpg)

The tour typically includes a quick stop for photos and an intro guided talk (about **20 minutes**). That first chunk is useful because it frames what you’re about to see. Buenos Aires has a lot of self-invented images floating around in people’s heads. Here, the guide pulls you back to the real contrast: **San Telmo feels Spanish-colonial and older**, so it doesn’t match the typical Paris-in-your-head version of the city.

## San Telmo Market: a taste of street-level Buenos Aires

![SAN TELMO + CAMINITO THE LOCAL WALKING TOUR! - San Telmo Market: a taste of street-level Buenos Aires](https://9.buenosairestravelguide.com/wp-content/uploads/san-telmo-caminito-the-local-walking-tour-4.jpg)  
One of your early stops is the **San Telmo Market** for about **30 minutes**. Even if you don’t plan to buy much, this is a great place for perspective. Markets tell you how locals shop, snack, and move through the day, and this one lines up with the tour’s theme: tradition with present-day life.

![SAN TELMO + CAMINITO THE LOCAL WALKING TOUR! - San Telmo Market: a taste of street-level Buenos Aires](https://9.buenosairestravelguide.com/wp-content/uploads/san-telmo-caminito-the-local-walking-tour-4.jpg)

The tour includes time for you to explore and choose your own small bite. You can eat **empanadas** here, but food isn’t included, so think of this as your chance to try something local without turning it into a full meal. If you’ve ever felt annoyed on tours when every stop is “pay extra,” this one is at least honest about giving you a moment to eat if you want.
